Send the gage out for a second calibration before use
Run a measurement system analysis before trusting it
Enter the sticker due date as the gage study result

explanation: A current calibration sticker says the gage was checked against a reference and found inside its calibration limits on that date. It does not show how much of the observed spread on this length comes from repeatability and reproducibility in actual use. The baseline still needs a measurement system analysis before those readings are trusted.

distractorExplanations.a: A current sticker documents a calibration check against a standard. It leaves repeatability and reproducibility on the shop floor unknown.
distractorExplanations.b: Another trip to calibration repeats the reference check. The open question is measurement variation in use, which a new sticker does not answer.
distractorExplanations.d: The due date on a sticker is a calendar fact about the last calibration. It is not a gage R&R percentage and cannot stand in for one.

prompt: A three-step assembly records first-pass yield at each step: leak test 50 percent, torque 80 percent, and label check 90 percent. Rework hides many failures before the next step. What is the rolled throughput yield of this line?

options.text: 36 percent, the product of the three step yields
50 percent, the leak-test first-pass yield by itself
80 percent, the torque-step first-pass yield by itself
90 percent, the label-check first-pass yield by itself

explanation: Rolled throughput yield multiplies the step first-pass yields: 0.50 times 0.80 is 0.40, and 0.40 times 0.90 is 0.36, or 36 percent. That 36 percent is the chance a unit clears all three steps the first time. Quoting 50, 80, or 90 percent reports one step's first-pass yield and leaves the other two steps out of the product. Rework can make end-of-line yield look healthier than this rolled figure.

distractorExplanations.b: Fifty percent is the leak-test first-pass yield by itself. Rolled throughput yield multiplies every step, so one step's yield is not the line result.
distractorExplanations.c: Eighty percent is the torque step by itself. The leak-test and label yields still have to be multiplied in, and they pull the rolled figure below 80 percent.
distractorExplanations.d: Ninety percent is the label check, the best of the three steps. A strong last step does not erase units that failed leak test or torque the first time.

prompt: Inspectors checked 250 welded frames and logged 20 defects. Each frame has 4 defect opportunities. The champion asks for defects per million opportunities on this lot. Which figure is the DPMO?

options.text: 0.02, defects divided by units times opportunities
0.08, defects divided by the 250 frames in the lot
80, that per-frame defect rate scaled per thousand frames
20,000 defects per million opportunities on the lot

explanation: Total opportunities are 250 frames times 4 per frame, which is 1,000. Defects per opportunity are 20 divided by 1,000, or 0.02. DPMO multiplies that rate by 1,000,000, so 0.02 times 1,000,000 is 20,000. Defects per unit are 20 divided by 250, or 0.08. The figure 0.08 looks smaller than 20,000 only because a per-unit rate is not multiplied by 1,000,000. Skipping the 4 opportunities moves the rate the other way: 0.08 is four times the 0.02 defects per opportunity.

distractorExplanations.a: 0.02 is defects per opportunity, 20 divided by 1,000. DPMO still multiplies that rate by 1,000,000, which is the step this figure skips.
distractorExplanations.b: 0.08 is defects per unit, 20 divided by 250. It looks smaller than 20,000 only because it is not scaled per million. Leaving out the 4 opportunities makes 0.08 larger than 0.02, so that omission is not what shrinks the figure.
distractorExplanations.c: 80 scales the 0.08 defects per unit by 1,000, as if the rate were per thousand frames. It still ignores opportunities and uses the wrong multiplier for a per-million rate.

prompt: A packing cell has 450 minutes available today and customer demand of 90 units. The bottleneck cycle time is 7 minutes per unit. What does that comparison mean for meeting this shift's demand?

options.text: Spare capacity remains, because takt time is the 7 minutes
This shift misses demand, because cycle time exceeds takt
This shift meets demand, because 7 minutes is a safe takt
Raise customer demand so takt climbs past the 7-minute cycle

explanation: Takt time is available time divided by demand: 450 divided by 90 is 5 minutes per unit. Cycle time at the bottleneck is 7 minutes, which is longer than that 5-minute takt. The cell needs 7 minutes to finish a unit while the customer requires one every 5 minutes, so this shift cannot meet demand. Working faster would cut cycle time; it would not change takt. Raising demand would make takt shorter than 5 minutes and widen the gap.

distractorExplanations.a: Seven minutes is the cycle time, not takt. Takt is 450 divided by 90, or 5 minutes, so the bottleneck is slower than the required pace rather than ahead of it.
distractorExplanations.c: Calling 7 minutes the takt swaps the two words. The customer pace is 5 minutes, and a 7-minute cycle does not meet that pace.
distractorExplanations.d: Takt equals available time divided by demand. Raising demand lowers takt, so the gap against a 7-minute cycle gets wider, not smaller.

prompt: End-of-line test on a wiring harness records pass or fail and nothing else. Last week 24 of 800 harnesses failed. A manager asks for the Cpk of that test. What should the Green Belt tell the tollgate?

Compute a Cpk after coding fails as 0 and passes as 1
Report no Cpk; the data are a proportion defective
Quote a Cp instead, since a fail rate has no center to judge

explanation: Cpk compares a continuous distribution with specification limits, using a process sigma. These records are pass or fail. The proportion defective is 24 divided by 800, or 0.03, and that proportion has no measured diameter and no spec width to put into a capability formula. Report the proportion, a yield, or a p-chart. Keep Cp and Cpk for variables data.

distractorExplanations.a: Looking up 3 percent defective on a normal table invents a variables index. These rows are attributes, with no sigma and no pair of specification limits.
distractorExplanations.b: Coding fails as 0 and passes as 1 invents a scale this pass-fail test does not measure. Cpk needs continuous readings, a sigma, and specification limits.
distractorExplanations.d: Cp is still a variables capability index, (USL minus LSL) divided by 6 short-term sigma. Switching from Cpk to Cp does not turn a proportion into a measured distribution.

prompt: Diameters from a stable grinding job bend away from the straight line on a normal probability plot. A teammate still wants to publish a normality-based Cpk at the tollgate. What should the Green Belt do with that index?

options.text: Withhold the Cpk while the probability plot bends
Publish the Cpk and call the bend a small-sample wiggle
Drop the bending tail points, then publish the Cpk
Read the bend itself as capability against the specifications

explanation: A normality-based Cpk describes how a normal curve sits between the specification limits. On this plot the points curve off the reference line, so the diameters do not follow that normal shape, even though the process is stable. Publishing the index would describe a distribution the grinder is not producing. The shape has to be handled with a fitting method before a capability number is quoted. A straight plot was the assumption, and this plot is not straight.

distractorExplanations.b: A bend away from the reference line is evidence against a normal shape. It is not a harmless small-sample wiggle that can be ignored while a normal Cpk is published.
distractorExplanations.c: Deleting tail points to force a straighter line hides the shape the process actually has. The index would then describe the edited sample, not the grind.
distractorExplanations.d: The curve of the plot speaks to distribution shape. It is not a comparison of process spread with the specification limits.

prompt: A honed bore is stable. The lower specification is 20.00 mm, the target is 20.15 mm, and the upper specification is 20.60 mm. Short-term sigma is 0.05 mm. Which reported value is Cp?

options.text: 0.5, using target minus the lower spec over 6 sigma
1.0, using half the specification width over 6 sigma
1.5, using the upper spec minus the target over 6 sigma
2.0, using upper spec minus lower spec over 6 sigma

explanation: Cp divides the full specification width by 6 times short-term sigma. The width is USL minus LSL: 20.60 minus 20.00 is 0.60 mm. Six times 0.05 mm is 0.30 mm. Cp is 0.60 divided by 0.30, which is 2.0. The target is not in that formula. Target minus LSL is 0.15, half the width is 0.30, and USL minus the target is 0.45; dividing those by 0.30 gives 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5, none of which is Cp.

distractorExplanations.a: 0.5 uses 20.15 minus 20.00, which is 0.15, then divides by 0.30. That numerator is target minus the lower spec, and Cp uses USL minus LSL.
distractorExplanations.b: 1.0 uses half of 0.60, which is 0.30, divided by 0.30. Cp keeps the full width of 0.60 mm in the numerator, not half of it.
distractorExplanations.c: 1.5 uses 20.60 minus 20.15, which is 0.45, then divides by 0.30. That is the upper spec minus the target. Cp does not subtract the target.

prompt: Rational subgroups of five are in hand for a stable shaft diameter, and the tollgate wants Cp. One analyst starts from the standard deviation of every measured point pooled together. Which spread belongs in that Cp?

options.text: The standard deviation of all points pooled as one set
The within-subgroup spread of those groups of five
The gap between the lower specification and the upper
The range from the lowest shift average to the highest

explanation: Cp is built on short-term sigma. With rational subgroups, that sigma comes from the variation inside the subgroups, such as the average range divided by d2. The standard deviation of every point pooled together also includes shift-to-shift movement, so it estimates overall, long-term sigma, the spread used in Pp and Ppk. The distance between the specification limits is the numerator of Cp, not the sigma.

distractorExplanations.a: Pooling every point into one standard deviation estimates overall, long-term sigma. Pp and Ppk use that spread. Cp needs the short-term sigma from inside the subgroups.
distractorExplanations.c: The distance from the lower spec to the upper spec is the tolerance width in the Cp numerator. It is a customer requirement, not an estimate of process sigma.
distractorExplanations.d: Differences among shift averages are between-subgroup movement. That movement sits in the long-term picture, not in the within-subgroup sigma that Cp uses.

prompt: Weld strength on a seat bracket is measured by pulling the bracket until it breaks, so each part can be tested one time. Three operators will each pull brackets from their own stack. Which gage study fits this test?

options.text: A crossed study, with every operator pulling the same brackets
No study at all, because a breaking test has no measurement error
A nested study, because a broken part cannot be crossed
A bias study that pulls each broken bracket again versus a master

explanation: A crossed gage study needs every operator to measure the same parts, so operator and part are crossed. This pull destroys the bracket, and each part can be measured one time, so the same bracket cannot be handed to the next operator. Parts are nested within operator, and the matching study is a nested measurement-system study. A destructive test still contains measurement error; destroying the part does not remove it.

distractorExplanations.a: Crossing operators on the same brackets requires each bracket to be pulled more than once. The test breaks the part, so that layout cannot be run.
distractorExplanations.b: A result that destroys the part still includes measurement error from the method, the setup, and the operator. Skipping the study leaves that error mixed into the strength numbers.
distractorExplanations.d: The broken bracket cannot be pulled a second time, and bias versus a master is a different question from how operators and parts contribute variation.

prompt: On this caliper study, percent of tolerance is 8 and percent of study variation is 42. The plant scores acceptance from percent of study variation: under 10 percent acceptable, 10 to 30 percent marginal, and over 30 percent unacceptable. What decision does that rule require?

options.text: Unacceptable, because study variation is 42 percent
Acceptable, because percent of tolerance is 8 percent
Marginal, because 8 and 42 average to 25 percent
Marginal, because 42 percent is a little past 30 percent

explanation: The plant's rule scores percent of study variation, and 42 is over 30, so the gage is unacceptable under that rule. Percent of tolerance is 8, inside the band the plant would call acceptable, because the tolerance is wide relative to the gage error. That second percentage is not the one this rule uses. Averaging the two gives (8 plus 42) divided by 2, which is 25 and would look marginal, but the rule does not average them.

distractorExplanations.b: Eight percent of tolerance sits under 10 and looks acceptable because the tolerance is wide. The plant's rule scores study variation, and 42 percent is over 30.
distractorExplanations.c: The average of 8 and 42 is 25, which would sit in the marginal band. The rule does not average the two percentages; it scores study variation, and 42 is over 30.
distractorExplanations.d: Forty-two percent of study variation is twelve points past the plant's 30 percent line. The rule calls that unacceptable, and it does not soften a miss into the marginal band.

prompt: When a diameter falls outside the specification, the supervisor measures that same part again until one reading falls inside the specification. Those later readings are offered for the gage study. What should the Green Belt do with them?

options.text: Keep the passing repeats and drop each earlier reading
Average each string of repeats into one study point
Count the repeats as reproducibility of the two people
Leave those until-it-passes repeats out of the study

explanation: A measurement system analysis needs the readings the gage and the people actually produce, including readings that miss the specification. Measuring again until a number passes selects on the outcome and makes the gage look better than it is. Those selected repeats do not belong in the study. Use a planned set of readings in which every assigned measurement is kept.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping the passing repeats and dropping the earlier readings is the selection itself. The study would then describe a filtered set of numbers, not the measurement system.
distractorExplanations.b: Averaging the tries blends a missed reading with later passes. The study would still rest on data collected by hunting for a number inside the specification.
distractorExplanations.c: Two people touching the gage is not a reproducibility study when the second person continues until the specification is met. Those repeats are selected, not a planned operator comparison.

prompt: A coating-line team fixed alpha at 0.05 before comparing two defect rates. The two-sample test returned p = 0.03. At the Analyze tollgate, what should the Green Belt tell the champion?

options.text: Fail to reject the null, because 0.03 sits too close to the preset alpha of 0.05.
Reject the null and tell the champion the gap is large enough to change the process.
Reject the null; a p-value below alpha does not show a useful effect.
Lower alpha to 0.03 after seeing p so the result can stay an open call.

explanation: Alpha was set at 0.05 before the data were examined, and p = 0.03 is below that alpha, so the team rejects H0. Rejection means a difference was detected. It does not say whether the size of the change is large enough for the champion to spend money on.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a p-value near alpha with a non-rejection; 0.03 is below the preset 0.05, so H0 is rejected.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats a statistically significant result as if it already showed the change is large enough to act on.
distractorExplanations.d: Alpha is locked before the p-value is known; sliding it down to equal p is not a valid decision rule.

prompt: On independent lots, a furnace trial compared a new setpoint with the current one at alpha 0.05. The test failed to reject the null, and the team discarded the change. A later study showed the setpoint really did cut scrap. Which error was the first call?

options.text: A Type I error: the team rejected a true null and kept a setpoint change that did nothing.
A Type I error: discarding the change after a non-significant test is the alpha risk they set.
No decision error: failing to reject the null proves the new setpoint has no scrap effect.
A Type II error: the test missed a scrap difference that later proved real.

explanation: Type I error is rejecting a true null, which is the alpha risk. Type II error is failing to reject a false null, which is beta. The first test kept H0, and a later study showed the setpoint really cut scrap, so that null was false. Missing a difference that was there is a Type II error.

distractorExplanations.a: Type I would mean they rejected a true null and adopted a useless change; this team kept H0 instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses alpha with the miss; discarding a real improvement after a non-rejection is beta, not alpha.
distractorExplanations.c: A non-significant result does not prove the null; it means this test failed to detect a difference.

As a reason to raise the upper control limit to the customer's maximum defect rate
As a reason to drop the p-chart and plot distance to the specification instead

explanation: The upper control limit on a p-chart is calculated from the process proportion, not from the customer's allowance. A point above that limit is a special-cause signal even when the day's percent is still inside the specification. The customer limit answers whether the rate is acceptable to the customer. The control limit answers whether Tuesday's rate is unusual for this process.

distractorExplanations.b: Staying under the customer's maximum means the day met the spec. The point is still outside the process control limit.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving the control limit up to the specification replaces a process statistic with the customer's allowance.
distractorExplanations.d: The p-chart is already the right chart for a proportion. The signal is the point beyond its limit, not a missing specification scale.

prompt: An operator wrote a faster kit-staging method on a suggestion slip during the shift. The crew is still staging kits the old way. A supervisor wants that slip listed as standard work on this week's control plan. What is the status of the idea?

options.text: It is already standard work because the slip sits in the suggestion box
It is standard work once the slip is pinned on the board, with no training given
It is not standard work until the crew agrees, documents, and trains to it
It is standard work as soon as a manager initials the slip and files it in the project folder

explanation: Standard work is the method the people who do the job have agreed to follow, written so the steps are clear, and taught so the next person can run it the same way. A suggestion is a proposal. Until the crew agrees, the method is documented, and people are trained, the control plan has nothing stable to hold.

distractorExplanations.a: A slip in a box is an idea waiting for review. Agreement, documentation, and training have not happened.
distractorExplanations.b: Pinning the slip displays the idea. People who have not been trained do not yet share one method.
distractorExplanations.d: A manager's initials record a review. They do not make an untried, untaught method the agreed standard.

prompt: A molding cell changes molds several times a shift. Its control plan lists one check: the supervisor reads the monthly scrap report. Before the Control tollgate, which check should the plan include?

options.text: The monthly scrap report by itself, since that total already gathers every defect the presses made
A first-piece check each time a run starts, kept on the plan beside the monthly scrap report
A quarterly reading of the scrap report, with no look at pieces when a run starts
A once-a-year scrap audit that replaces both startup checks and the monthly report

explanation: A control plan puts a check where the process can still be corrected. The first piece of a run shows whether the setup is right before a shift of molds is made. The monthly scrap report totals damage after the fact and can stay as a lagging view. Stretching that report to a quarter or a year removes the startup check the plan was missing.

distractorExplanations.a: The monthly total is lagging. It does not look at the first piece before the rest of the run is made.
distractorExplanations.c: A quarterly scrap reading is even later than the monthly report and still skips the startup piece.
distractorExplanations.d: An annual audit summarizes old scrap. It removes the in-process check instead of adding the first-piece look.

prompt: A two-level trial changed oven temperature and held every other factor fixed. Average defects were 48 at the low setting and 36 at the high setting. Which statement does that comparison support?

options.text: Each setting is credited with half of the gap between the two averages
The midpoint temperature is the optimum, so the gap is not reported as a main effect
No main effect can be stated until a third, untested factor is folded into the trial
The main effect is 12 fewer defects, computed as 48 at low minus 36 at high

explanation: With every other factor held fixed, the main effect of temperature is the difference of the two averages: 48 − 36 = 12. The high setting averages 12 fewer defects than the low setting. Two averages do not locate a best point between the settings, and they do not have to be split in half or withheld until another factor is added.

distractorExplanations.a: The main effect is the full gap between the level averages, 12, not half of that gap.
distractorExplanations.b: A midpoint optimum is not identified by two averages. The comparison supports a main effect of 12, not a response-surface peak.
distractorExplanations.c: The other factors were held fixed, so this two-level gap is already the main effect of temperature.

prompt: Weeks after the Improve pilot, the line still sorts every piece while the new control plan sits unused. The chart has held the gain, with no special-cause signal. What should the team do next with the sort and the plan?

options.text: Audit the control plan on a cadence and retire the blanket sort once the gain holds
Keep sorting every piece as the standing method and leave the control plan unaudited
End the sort and the plan audits together on the day the tollgate signature is dry
Add a second sort station downstream and cancel any scheduled audit of the control plan

explanation: Sorting every piece is containment while the team proves the gain. Once the chart shows the process holding, the ongoing method is the control plan, checked on an audit cadence so the standard does not drift. Leaving a sort of every piece in place makes inspection the control system. Dropping both the sort and the audits at the tollgate leaves nothing watching the process.

distractorExplanations.b: A permanent sort of every piece replaces the control plan with inspection and skips the audit that holds the plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Signing the tollgate is not a reason to stop checking. The plan still needs an audit cadence after the sort comes off.
distractorExplanations.d: A second sort station adds more inspection. Canceling the audit removes the check on the control plan.

prompt: The new work standard is written, but a scheduling rule still stops the crew from following it. The Green Belt leads the project part time and will not stay to run the line after the Control tollgate. Who is supposed to clear that rule?

options.text: The Green Belt, by moving onto the line full time once the tollgate is signed
The Black Belt, by taking the process owner's daily job on that line
The champion, who clears the scheduling barrier that blocks the new standard
The process owner, by handing daily running of the line back to the Green Belt

explanation: The champion sponsors the project and clears barriers the team cannot remove, including a scheduling rule that blocks the new standard. A Green Belt usually leads the project part time and does not stay on the line full time after Control. The process owner runs the process from that point. A Black Belt may coach the project and does not take the owner's daily job.

distractorExplanations.a: The Green Belt leads part time. Staying on the line full time after Control is not that role, and it does not clear the scheduling rule.
distractorExplanations.b: A Black Belt coaches or leads the larger project. The process owner's daily job stays with the process owner.
distractorExplanations.d: After Control the process owner runs the process. Handing the line back to the Green Belt reverses that handoff.
